item.title: ECB officials see December rate hike as uncertainty clouds 2027 outlook
item.description: Policymakers see December as the likeliest time for a rate increase, while rising bond yields, high energy costs, AI investment and uncertainty over US policy complicate the outlook for next year ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Jana Randow and Alexander Weber European Central Bank officials are preparing to finish 2026 with a third interest-rate increase, the last before an increasingly complex backdrop overshadows decisions next year. While policymakers speaking this week in Bangkok kept open the option of acting in October, they pointed to December as the more likely timing for a hike that’s also widely anticipated among traders and economists. But the discussions also revealed growing unease over issues including rising bond yields, high energy costs and the blistering investment boom in artificial intelligence.  “The tradeoffs for monetary policy are going to get more tricky,” Governing Council member Martins Kazaks said in an interview. “So far, the decisions have been relatively easy. But there’s a lot of uncertainty and very low visibility.” The gathering in the Thai capital was dominated by warnings that the economy’s surprising resilience to the Middle East conflict will come under increasing strain. The euro zone, where investors have pushed up France’s borrowing costs due to its gaping budget deficit and political gridlock, was a focal point.  US midterm elections and an unpredictable response from President Donald Trump are adding to the uncertainty. Policymakers signaled a preference for sticking with a quarterly pace of rate increases, suggesting continuity after being the first major central bank to hike rates since the war broke out. That would mean waiting until the Dec. 17 gathering, when they’ll have new economic forecasts.  “From a policymaker’s perspective, you want to take decisions when you have the largest amount of data available, and the next such meeting is December,” Governing Council member Gediminas Simkus said in a separate interview. “But you also can’t ignore the fact that we have a meeting in October.” On the bright side, the Lithuanian and his colleagues pointed out that inflation heading toward 4 per cent — double the ECB’s target — hasn’t yet spread widely. At the same time, there are no signs that energy-driven price pressures are letting up.   On Friday, Brent oil hit $110 a barrel for the first time since May after Iran-backed Houthi rebels pummeled Saudi Arabia with missile and drone strikes, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged tit-for-tat attacks on energy infrastructure. With wage negotiations looming next spring, the ECB is carefully analyzing how such shocks are “traveling through the economy,” President Christine Lagarde told CNN. “We are not seeing any of that yet, but we have to be extremely careful that little signs, indices of such secondary effects are visible.”  Officials are already pondering how restrictive monetary policy needs to become. The last two hikes, in June and September, took the deposit rate to the upper end of the range the ECB previously identified as neutral.  Additional moves — traders are betting on three by September next year — would start to damp economic activity just as a long-awaited recovery is taking hold.   “The market is pricing that we are going to have to do more,” Governing Council member Pierre Wunsch told Bloomberg TV. “It’s a base case that looks reasonable, but again, we are in a very uncertain world.” Some of that uncertainty is originating in Europe, with French finances in the spotlight after a bond-market selloff stoked memories of the sovereign-debt crisis that shook the region through much of the 2010s. Many participants in Bangkok, including IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva, argued that large budget deficits and debts must urgently be addressed, calling advanced economies the “worst offenders.”  While some ECB officials signaled optimism that the message investors sent to France has resonated with the government as it prepares key budget votes, others are already focused on how to respond if the situation deteriorates. “The toolbox allows for quite a lot of instruments,” said Governing Council member Martin Kocher. “We are not at the stage where we need to discuss any of these instruments. But they are there if they are needed.” The ECB’s work is overshadowed by increasing frustration among officials about Lagarde’s refusal to offer clarity on a possible early exit, according to people familiar with the matter.  The institution is in the midst of a major leadership overhaul, with Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel leaving in January, Chief Economist Philip Lane’s term expiring in May and Lagarde’s technically running through October 2027. Vice President Boris Vujcic joined in June.

item.title: Axis Bank Q2FY27 result: Profit rises 38% to ₹7,003 crore, misses estimates
item.description: Net interest income rose 11.8 per cent to ₹15,371 crore, while loans grew 23 per cent and provisions fell 52.2 per cent; other income declined 1.4 per cent to ₹6,531 crore ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Indian private-sector lender Axis Bank reported on Saturday a quarterly profit that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as higher operating expenses and weaker other income offset robust credit growth and lower provisions.Axis Bank, the country's third-largest private bank by assets, posted a stand-alone net profit of ₹7,003 crore ($737.5 million) for the quarter ended on September 30, compared with ₹5,090 crore a year earlier.Analysts, on average, had forecast a profit of ₹7,124 crore, according to LSEG-compiled data.Other income, which includes earnings from bonds and other investments, fell 1.4 per cent to ₹6,531 crore.Rising bond yields and volatility in the rupee during the quarter weighed on treasury income at the Mumbai-based lender, tempering earnings even as lending expanded across segments.Banks across India reported strong loan growth during the quarter across corporate and retail portfolios.Net interest income grew 11.8 per cent to ₹15,371 crore, helped by a 23 per cent rise in total loans. Deposits increased 20.7 per cent from a year earlier.Provisions for potential bad loans and other contingencies fell 52.2 per cent to ₹1,694 crore.The gross non-performing asset ratio stood at 1.16 per cent at end-September, compared with 1.28 per cent three months earlier.

item.title: Apple appoints Meta veteran Scott Tucker to lead global litigation
item.description: Tucker will oversee commercial and patent litigation worldwide and legal matters involving Apple's financial services as the company faces mounting lawsuits under General Counsel Jennifer Newstead ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Mark Gurman Apple Inc. has tapped a longtime Meta Platforms Inc. executive as its new litigation chief, bolstering its legal team at a time when the iPhone maker faces a growing array of lawsuits. The company has hired Scott Tucker, a longtime deputy general counsel and litigation chief at Meta, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The move reunites Tucker with new Apple General Counsel Jennifer Newstead, who is bringing on a trusted lieutenant from her time at the social networking giant. Tucker is becoming Apple’s vice president of global litigation and financial services, a newly created position overseeing commercial and patent litigation worldwide, said the people, who asked not to be named because the move isn’t public. He’ll also manage legal matters involving the company’s financial offerings.  The appointment means Heather Grenier, Apple’s current vice president of commercial and competition litigation, will move one level lower in the organisation, reporting to Tucker instead of directly to Newstead. Grenier will still remain on Newstead’s legal leadership team.  Tucker, in addition to his tenure at Meta, previously held a senior legal position at Morgan Stanley, giving him experience relevant to his new financial services responsibilities. Newstead took over as Apple’s general counsel in March after serving as Meta’s top lawyer for six years. Kyle Andeer, another senior member of Apple’s legal department and its longtime vice president managing regulatory and product-related legal matters, is seeing his role expand. He is gaining oversight of international legal matters and functions involving online child safety, cybersecurity and law enforcement. Spokespeople for Apple and Meta declined to comment.  The changes are part of a broader reorganisation under Newstead, who oversees legal and government affairs. Apple recently hired Nate Gatten, a former American Airlines Group Inc. executive, as its vice president of government affairs. The company has also appointed new government affairs leads for different international regions. Apple combined its legal and government affairs groups under Newstead following the recent retirements of Lisa Jackson, the former head of environmental, policy and social initiatives, and previous top lawyer Kate Adams. Former Chief Executive Officer Tim Cook, now the company’s executive chairman, has also taken a leading role in government affairs. Apple is waging a variety of legal battles, including a sweeping US antitrust lawsuit, its long-running dispute with Epic Games Inc. over App Store restrictions, and litigation related to privacy and delays to Siri features. The company has faced billions of dollars in judgments and settlements in recent years, while regulators in the US and Europe have challenged business practices central to the iPhone maker’s operations. Some Apple executives believe the company hasn’t fared as well in court as it should have, particularly in litigation involving the App Store. Those setbacks have forced Apple to change its commission structure and the circumstances under which it can charge developers. The changes threaten to significantly slow growth in Apple’s services business, a key driver of revenue expansion in recent years. A slowdown in that business would deal a major blow to the company’s overall financial performance. Even in the best of times, overseeing Apple’s litigation is a difficult job. The Cupertino, California-based company is among the most frequently sued businesses in the world, facing cases ranging from slip-and-fall claims at its retail stores to multibillion-dollar antitrust disputes. Grenier took over the role under particularly challenging circumstances, replacing her predecessor just before Apple’s landmark trial against Epic Games began in 2021. Her tenure has also spanned two major leadership transitions: the appointment of John Ternus as CEO and Newstead’s arrival. In recent weeks, Ternus has overseen a sweeping series of executive changes, including the appointment of new leaders for the App Store, events and corporate functions such as information security and real estate. The reshuffling also includes the departure of the longtime Apple Pay chief, the replacement of the company’s mergers and acquisitions head, and a reorganisation of the company’s hardware engineering division.

item.title: Satcom row: Starlink says India infra has govt approvals, ready for launch
item.description: Musk-led Starlink says it has built dedicated infrastructure with requisite govt approvals after Reliance Industries welcomed satcom competition but stressed that all operators must comply with laws ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / Satcom row: Starlink says India infra has govt approvals, ready for launch

Satcom row: Starlink says India infra has govt approvals, ready for launch Musk-led Starlink says it has built dedicated infrastructure with requisite govt approvals after Reliance Industries welcomed satcom competition but stressed that all operators must comply with laws

Starlink further said it was ready to connect India with high-speed internet (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Oct 17 2026 | 9:01 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Starlink on Friday said it has worked with Indian regulators, industry and operators for over five years and built dedicated infrastructure in the country "all with the requisite government approvals", as the Elon Musk-led company asserted its readiness to provide high-speed internet services in India.   ALSO READ: Satcom row: Reliance welcomes competition, says Indian laws apply to all Starlink's post on X also tagged Reliance Industries' statement issued earlier Friday, in which the Mukesh Ambani-led company said it welcomed competition in satellite communications, including from Starlink, but stressed that all players must comply with Indian laws. Starlink responded on X saying: "We have worked closely with regulators, industry and operators in India for 5+ years, and built a network of dedicated systems, gateways, and other infrastructure all in-country to exclusively serve Indian traffic safely and securely - and all with the requisite government approvals."   Starlink further said it was ready to connect India with high-speed internet.   Friday's exchange comes amid a public spat over competition in India's satellite communications market, with Musk criticising the country's satcom landscape and raising questions about the competitive environment. Reliance said it sees a competitive market as the true test of which player serves customers best, and asserted that every company operating in India must follow the law. In its first direct response to Musk's recent barbs, Reliance on Friday said it was placing "the facts on record."   "At Reliance, we have never feared competition. We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best," the company said in a statement. Also Read

Satcom row: Reliance welcomes competition, says Indian laws apply to all

Reliance backed its stance citing Jio's own record. Jio entered India's crowded telecom market in 2016 as the newest player, with not a single customer, and in a matter of just ten years, earned the trust of over 530 million customers, offering Indians some of the best digital infrastructure and most affordable data in the world, it said. "We welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink. Every player, Jio included, must serve the people of India and abide by the laws and policies of the land," Reliance's statement said. It further said India's openness to investment and innovation, homegrown or international, rests on the rule of law. "Like every Indian enterprise, Reliance has grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international, that improve the lives of the people. That openness rests on the rule of law," it said. As the government has maintained, it applies the same process to every applicant, Indian or foreign, Reliance said, adding "Jio's own satellite services await clearances". Government sources, responding to the controversy surrounding Starlink and Musk's recent claims, have already made it clear that any company operating in India must comply with the law of the land. The Centre's position has been clear and consistent throughout, they added. "Government's position has been very clear, and was so even at the time they had applied, that if you don't follow Indian laws, you cannot do business here...So to do business here, you have to follow Indian laws," sources had said earlier this week. Recently at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, Bharti Airtel Chairman Sunil Mittal said his satellite communications venture Eutelsat OneWeb was significantly ahead of Elon Musk's Starlink in the queue to launch services in India -- his remarks adding a fresh twist to a public dispute over regulatory approvals and competition in the country's satellite internet market. "I think I am significantly ahead in the queue from him. I applied five years back," Mittal said. "We don't have the permission, so we'll be very happy to get it at least a few days before him". Mittal said OneWeb's ground network has been ready for three years, and its satellites have been hovering over India for five years, but the company is still awaiting permission to begin commercial operations. The pushback from Mittal, and now Reliance, came after Musk, the world's richest man, accused powerful business interests of blocking Starlink's entry into India. In a series of posts on social media platform X recently, Musk took aim at Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani, sarcastically addressing him as "Prime Minister Ambani" and questioning whether he wielded greater influence over India's decisions than Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Musk has alleged that some business groups are seeking to preserve a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers. However, the Ministry of Communications rejected the charge, describing suggestions that the regulatory framework or its application was unfair or discriminatory as "baseless and misconceived". The government said satellite operators must meet the same regulatory requirements, including security conditions and spectrum allocation rules, before they can begin commercial services. Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said three ventures -- Musk's Starlink, Reliance's Jio Satcom and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb -- had secured satellite communications licences. Amazon's Project Kuiper has expressed interest but must follow the established procedure, he said. Scindia made it clear that spectrum would be assigned once the government finalised a revenue-based charging framework and individual operators fulfilled security requirements. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) and the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) were close to a decision on satellite spectrum pricing, he had added. The distinction between a licence and operational approval is central to the dispute: securing a licence does not automatically allow a company to begin commercial services. Spectrum assignment and the fulfilment of security conditions remain key steps. The dispute comes at a consequential time for Reliance, which is preparing for the initial public offering of Jio Platforms, its digital services business. Jio has set a price band of Rs 1,065 to 1,119 a share for its offer of up to 27 crore new shares, about 3 per cent of the existing capital, with no offer-for-sale component. At the top of the band, the sale would raise about Rs 30,213 crore, ahead of Hyundai Motor India's Rs 27,870 crore share sale in October 2024, the country's biggest. The price implies a market value of about Rs 10.3 lakh crore, short of the roughly Rs 11 lakh crore the company had earlier been said to seek. Bidding runs from October 21 to 23, with anchor investors bidding on October 19. The shares are expected to begin trading on October 28. Reliance is also developing its satellite ambitions, including a proposed constellation of about 1,600 low-earth-orbit satellites aimed at extending internet connectivity to 600,000 villages. That would put Jio in more direct competition with Starlink, which is seeking access to a vast market where satellite broadband could serve remote communities and locations poorly covered by terrestrial networks. Ironically, Reliance and SpaceX last year signed an agreement to explore ways of bringing Starlink services to Indian customers through Jio's retail network.
